curator.photoShows: Dumbbell_Bench_Press: flat bench, two dumbbells, both arms at the chest in frame 0 and both locked out in frame 1 (simultaneous two-arm). One_Arm_Dumbbell_Bench_Press: flat bench, one dumbbell, other arm idle. Alternating_Floor_Press: two kettlebells, lying on the floor, one arm locked out and the other lowered. Dumbbell_Bench_Press_with_Neutral_Grip: flat bench, two dumbbells moving together with a neutral grip.
curator.why: None of the sources shows an alternating dumbbell press on a bench, with one dumbbell held locked out while the other is lowered. Dumbbell_Bench_Press is the two-arm photo that was already rejected. One_Arm_Dumbbell_Bench_Press is single-arm with no second dumbbell, and the neutral-grip version is two-arm simultaneous. Alternating_Floor_Press does alternate, but it uses kettlebells and is done on the floor rather than a bench, so both the implement and the body position are wrong.

curator.photoShows: Seated lever-arm chest press machine of the Hammer-Strength type (front view), with plates faintly visible behind the lever arms. Bilateral horizontal press. Frame 0: handles at mid-chest with elbows back. Frame 1: arms extended forward.
curator.why: The source instructions say to 'Load an appropriate weight onto the pins', so this is a plate-loaded lever chest press, which is exactly what the app name describes: seated, flat (not incline or decline), two-arm horizontal press. Machine_Bench_Press was rejected because it is a selectorized stack machine ('select the weight'), not plate-loaded. Leverage_Incline_Chest_Press and Leverage_Decline_Chest_Press are angled variations, so the flat Leverage_Chest_Press is the correct choice.

reviewers.reason: I viewed both frames. They show a seated, plate-loaded lever-arm chest press machine of the Hammer-Strength type. Dark weight plates sit on the lever arms behind the handles in frame 0, the machine frame reads 'LEVER...' in frame 1, and the source instructions say to 'Load an appropriate weight onto the pins', so it is plate-loaded and not a stack machine. The athlete sits upright with his back against the pad and uses both arms at once on neutral or pronated handles, pressing horizontally. Frame 0 has the handles beside the mid-chest with elbows back. Frame 1 has the arms extended forward at chest height. Implement, body position, laterality and movement all match the app's Plate-Loaded Chest Press, and copying the two frames gives a correct rep.

I viewed both frames. The athlete sits upright, chest up and back against the pad, in a selectorized-looking frame that is in fact a plate-loaded lever-arm chest press: black plates sit on the horns behind each arm (lower left and lower right of frame 0), the base reads 'LEVE[RAGE]' in frame 1, and the source tells you to load weight onto the pins. Frame 0: horizontal pronated grips beside the mid-chest, elbows back and out. Frame 1: elbows fully extended and the handles converge in front of the sternum at chest height. Both arms press at the same time on a horizontal path, with elbow extension and shoulder horizontal flexion. That is a press, not a fly, because the elbows go from bent to straight rather than staying fixed. It is also flat, not incline or decline (the source keeps separate Leverage Incline and Decline entries). The implement, laterality, seated position and movement all match a generic plate-loaded (Hammer-Strength-style) chest press.

curator.photoShows: Cable_Chest_Press: seated, two handles, both arms pressing together. Standing_Cable_Chest_Press: standing between dual pulleys with stirrup handles, both arms pressing. Incline_Cable_Chest_Press: incline bench, two handles, both arms. Single-Arm_Cable_Crossover: high-pulley fly with one arm opening out while the other holds.
curator.why: Every cable chest press in the source is two-arm, which is the flaw already rejected for this exercise. The only single-arm cable chest exercise, Single-Arm_Cable_Crossover, is a fly done in an alternating pattern, not a press. No source shows a one-arm cable press.

curator.photoShows: Standing, bodyweight stance, two weight plates squeezed together between flat palms. Frame 0: plates held at the chest with elbows bent. Frame 1: arms extended straight out in front at chest height, still squeezing the plates.
curator.why: The Svend press is the standard exercise called the plate squeeze press (some apps list it as 'Plate Squeeze (Svend Press)'). In both, you squeeze plates between your palms and press them horizontally away from the chest, which fits the app's chest, horizontal-push and bracing tags. Isometric_Chest_Squeezes uses no plates and has no press. Confidence is medium because some coaches use 'plate squeeze press' for a version lying on a bench. If the app means that version, this standing photo would be the wrong body position.

reviewers.reason: I viewed both frames. He stands with feet about hip-width apart and holds two weight plates pressed together between flat palms, using both arms and no other load. Frame 0: plates at mid-chest, elbows bent and flared. Frame 1: arms extended straight out in front at chest height, still squeezing the plates. 'Plate Squeeze Press' is the standard alternative name for the Svend press, and the implement (plates squeezed together), standing position, two-arm action and horizontal press path all match. No bench or lying variation is implied by the app name.

I viewed both frames. The athlete stands with feet about hip-width, wears no other load, and holds two plates squeezed together between flat, open palms with fingers pointing forward. Frame 0: plates pressed against the lower chest with elbows bent and flared. Frame 1: arms extended straight forward at chest height, palms still pressed flat against the plates. The plates travel out horizontally from the chest; they are not raised in an arc, so this is not a front plate raise. The plates are squeezed, not gripped by the rim, which is what makes it a squeeze press. This is the Svend press, i.e. the plate squeeze press: same implement (two plates held together), both arms, standing, horizontal press path.

curator.photoShows: Bodyweight push-up on the gym floor, three-quarter side view. Hands about shoulder width or a little wider, feet together on the floor, body straight, no load. Frame 0: arms locked out at the top. Frame 1: chest lowered almost to the floor.
curator.why: This is the standard floor push-up with full range, a neutral hand width, feet on the floor and no load, which is exactly the generic exercise. Push-Up_Wide shows a wide grip from the front, and Pushups_Close_and_Wide_Hand_Positions uses a close hand position with frame 0 at the bottom, so neither is the plain version. Clock_Push-Up looks like a plain push-up but is a different source exercise. Pushups is the clearest canonical photo.

reviewers.reason: I viewed both frames. They show a bodyweight push-up on a flat rubber gym floor, seen in three-quarter side view. Hands are flat on the floor about shoulder width or a little wider, feet together on the floor, nothing elevated and no load. Frame 0 has the arms locked out with the body in a plank (hips at most slightly high). Frame 1 has the elbows bent and the chest and face just above the floor, with hands and feet in the same places. Implement, laterality, body position, support surface, load and range all match a standard push-up, so someone copying these two frames would do the app exercise.

I viewed both frames. They show a bodyweight push-up on the gym floor with nothing added: hands flat on the floor at about shoulder width or a little wider, feet together on the floor, and the body held in a straight plank with no load. Frame 0 shows the arms locked out at the top. In frame 1 the elbows bend, the arms angle back and out, and the chest and face come down almost to the floor. The movement is a full-range horizontal push from lockout to chest near the floor, with no incline, decline, deficit, knee support or plyometric part. Someone copying these two frames would do a standard push-up. The source text puts the hands 36 inches apart, but the photo shows an ordinary grip, and grip width counts as an acceptable difference. In frame 0 the hips look slightly high, but that comes from the low three-quarter camera angle, and the plank is clearly straight in frame 1.

curator.photoShows: Closest is Isometric_Wipers. Bodyweight, very wide hands on the floor, front-oblique view. Frame 0: low and shifted toward the right hand, right elbow bent, left arm angled out fairly straight (an archer-like bottom). Frame 1: centred at mid-low depth with both elbows bent. Neither frame shows the top with both arms straight.
curator.why: Isometric Wipers is a low side-to-side 'wiper' (typewriter) push-up, not an archer push-up. An archer rep starts at the top with both arms straight and wide, lowers toward one hand while the other arm stays straight, then presses back to lockout. The wiper pair never shows a straight-arm top. Its second frame is a centred, bent-arm position that is not part of an archer rep, so copying the two frames teaches staying low and sliding across, a different range and progression. Single-Arm_Push-Up has the free hand behind the back, so it is a one-arm push-up, not an archer. Push-Up_Wide is a symmetric wide push-up, Plyo_Kettlebell_Pushups is a kettlebell crossover, and Clock_Push-Up shows a plain push-up. A curator who treats typewriter push-ups as archer push-ups could revisit Isometric_Wipers, whose frame 0 alone is a credible archer bottom, but by the strict rule it is a near miss.

curator.photoShows: Closest is Drop_Push, the source's own depth push-up. Frame 0: hands on two plyo boxes, arms straight, feet on the floor. Frame 1: hands still on the boxes, chest lowered between them below box height. There is no drop to the floor, no catch and no airborne phase. Incline_Push-Up_Depth_Jump: feet up on a box, hands on the floor between two aerobic steps; frame 0 is the bottom, frame 1 is airborne.
curator.why: A depth push-up means dropping from elevated hand supports to the floor, absorbing the landing, and exploding back up. Drop_Push's instructions describe that, but its frames only show a controlled lowering with the hands staying on the boxes, so copying them gives a deficit push-up, not an explosive depth drop. Incline_Push-Up_Depth_Jump is explosive but uses a feet-elevated (decline) position the app name does not have, and it never shows the hands landing on the steps. Plyo_Push-up was already rejected as a floor plyo push-up, and its frames show no depth or air. Clock_Push-Up's frames look like a plain floor push-up. Plyo_Kettlebell_Pushups is a one-hand-on-kettlebell lateral crossover.

curator.photoShows: Bodyweight push-up with each hand on its own plyo box (two boxes about shoulder-width-plus apart), feet together on the floor, no load. Frame 0: arms straight at the top on the boxes. Frame 1: elbows bent, hands still on the boxes, chest and head lowered between them below the box tops, so the range goes past hand level.
curator.why: The frames show the defining feature of a deficit push-up: hands on raised platforms so the chest drops below hand level, through a full push-up range, with feet on the floor and no load. This fixes the earlier rejection, where a plain floor push-up had no deficit. Caveat: the boxes are fairly tall, so the body is moderately inclined (head higher than feet), more than a plate- or parallette-height deficit. The movement and range a copier would perform are still a deficit push-up. The source exercise is a plyometric drop push, but its frames never show the drop; they show only the deficit lowering. No other source photo shows a push-up below hand level: Push-Up_Wide, Pushups and Close-Grip_Push-Up_off_of_a_Dumbbell are floor push-ups or use a single raised support, and Incline_Push-Up_Depth_Jump has the feet elevated with the hands on the floor.

reviewers.reason: I viewed both frames. The hands are on two separate plyo boxes, each roughly 12 in (30 cm) tall with plates inside, and the feet are on the track floor. In frame 0 the shoulders are far above the feet, so the body slopes upward at a clear angle. That is an incline (hands-elevated) push-up set-up, not the level plank of a deficit push-up. In frame 1 the hands stay on the boxes and the head drops between them, but the chest only gets to about box-top (hand) height and the torso still slopes up from the feet. Someone copying these frames would do an easier hands-on-boxes incline push-up with at most a small extra drop below the hands. A coach's deficit push-up keeps the body level (low blocks, plates or handles, or feet raised to the same height) and takes the chest clearly below the hands. The source's actual exercise is also different: Drop Push is a plyometric drill in which the athlete pushes off the boxes and lands with the hands on the floor, and these frames are just posed positions from it. The photo fixes the earlier 'floor push-up' flaw but brings in a new body-position mismatch (incline, feet low), so it is not a safe match.

I viewed both frames, and they do not show the extra range that defines a deficit push-up. Each hand is on its own plyo box, roughly 30 to 45 cm tall, and the feet are together on the floor. Frame 0 shows the body clearly inclined, head end up, so this is an incline push-up setup. In frame 1 the near arm sits in the same plane as the red box. Its forearm is vertical, its upper arm is about horizontal, and the elbow is about 90 degrees, the same depth as a normal push-up. The near shoulder sits well above the box top, roughly a forearm's length (about 20 cm) above the hand, so the chest ends at or a little above hand level. Only the head, with the neck bent and face down, dips below the top of the far box. The defining part of a deficit push-up, the chest sinking past the hands with the body near horizontal, is not shown. Someone copying these frames would do an incline push-up on two high boxes to standard depth, which is easier than a floor push-up, while the app's Deficit Push-Up is a harder strength and hypertrophy progression. The source exercise is also a different one: Drop Push is a plyometric in which the hands push off the boxes and land on the floor between them. That drop is not shown, so the frames are only the box setup and a shallow lowering. The curator says the range goes past hand level, but the frames do not support that.

curator.photoShows: No source push-up photo shows external load (no plate on the back, vest, chains or band). Pushups is an unloaded floor push-up. In Plyo_Kettlebell_Pushups and Close-Grip_Push-Up_off_of_a_Dumbbell, the kettlebell or dumbbell is a hand support under the hand, not a load on the body.
curator.why: The app name needs a visible load on the athlete. Pushups was already rejected for being unweighted. A full-text search of fedb found no push-up with a plate, vest or chains. The only weights in push-up photos are hand supports, which do not load the body.

curator.photoShows: Spider_Crawl: bodyweight, prone on hands and toes, with both frames held at the BOTTOM of a push-up (elbows bent to about 90 degrees, chest low). Frame 0 has both feet on the floor. Frame 1 has one leg externally rotated with the knee drawn up to the same-side elbow. The arms are never straight in either frame.
curator.why: This is the closest candidate, but it is a different exercise. The source's own instructions say to hold the bent-arm (90 degree) position and alternate knee-to-elbow, a low-plank crawl drill. A Spiderman push-up starts with the arms straight, brings the knee to the elbow while lowering, then presses back up to lockout. The photos show no elbow extension or press, so someone copying them would do a low isometric knee-drive, not a push-up. The other candidates are wrong too: Mountain_Climbers and Groiners have arms straight and no push-up, Push_Up_to_Side_Plank is a rotation, and Pushups is a standard push-up with no knee drive, which is the base exercise for a named variation.

curator.photoShows: Bodyweight push-up on the floor with a wide hand placement. Frame 0: body lowered and shifted over one hand; that elbow is deeply flexed and the other arm is almost straight, the low side position of a typewriter. Frame 1: still low near the floor, now centred between the hands with both elbows bent, mid-way through the lateral shift at the bottom.
curator.why: The defining feature of a typewriter push-up is a wide-hand push-up where the athlete lowers over one hand (other arm straight) and travels sideways at the bottom toward the other hand. The two frames show exactly that: a low side position, then a low centre position, wide hands, unloaded, on the floor. Clock_Push-Up (plyo push-up rotating around a circle) and the plain Pushups photos are other exercises. Medium confidence for three reasons. The source text describes pushing back up between sides, but the frames clearly stay low. Neither frame shows the arms-straight top. And the source name ('wipers') differs, although it is the same side-to-side push-up pattern.

reviewers.reason: I viewed both frames. The set-up matches a typewriter push-up: an unloaded, prone push-up on the floor, on the toes with no elevation or deficit, hands placed well outside shoulder width, and no implement or load. Frame 0 shows the body low and shifted over the viewer's-left hand. That shoulder sits over the hand with the elbow bent, while the other (wristband) arm reaches out diagonally and is nearly straight. The head and chest are close to the floor, so this is the low lateral position of a typewriter. Frame 1 shows the body low and centred between the wide hands with both elbows bent about 90 degrees, which is the bottom of the slide. The source's text describes wipers that push back up between sides. However, neither frame shows a top position: both stay low and differ only by a sideways shift. Someone copying them would therefore shift side to side at the bottom, which is the typewriter pattern. Only one side is shown, which the rules accept. Laterality, stance, support surface and load all agree, and no other source in the list (Clock, Push-Up Wide, Single-Arm) fits better.

I viewed both frames. They show a bodyweight push-up on the floor with the hands set wide and no load. In frame 0 the chest and head are almost on the floor and the body is shifted over the image-left hand. That elbow is deeply bent and flared, and the image-right arm is nearly straight. In frame 1 the chest is at about the same low height, but the body has moved toward the image-right hand. Now the image-right elbow is deeply bent and the image-left arm is straight. So the two frames are the two low end positions of a sideways shift at the bottom, with the straight arm switching sides. That is the defining path of a typewriter push-up: a lateral move in the frontal plane at the bottom, not an up-and-down press. The implement (bodyweight), body position (prone plank, feet on the floor, no elevation), hand width and laterality (both hands loaded, shifting side to side) all match. One caveat: the source text for 'Isometric Wipers' says to push back up through the centre before dropping to the other side, which would make it a wiper or alternating archer push-up. But the photos only show two low positions on opposite sides. Someone copying frame 0 then frame 1 would stay low and slide across, which is the typewriter. Neither frame shows the arms-straight top position.

curator.photoShows: One-Arm_Long_Bar_Row: standing landmine row, one arm. The bar runs alongside his body and he faces the loaded end with feet roughly square. He grips the shaft just inside the plate, with no forearm on the knee. Bent_Over_One-Arm_Long_Bar_Row: the same parallel set-up with square feet, a neutral grip on the shaft behind the plate and the free hand on the knee.
curator.why: A Meadows row is a named variation of the one-arm landmine row. The lifter stands side-on to the bar in a staggered stance, braces the free forearm on the front knee, and grips the very end of the bar (the sleeve) overhand, rowing with the elbow flared. Both source photos show the standard one-arm landmine (long bar) row instead: bar running alongside the body, square stance, grip on the shaft. Under the rules, the base exercise cannot stand in for a named variation. Bent_Over_Two-Arm_Long_Bar_Row and T-Bar_Row_with_Handle are two-arm rows, so they are ruled out too.

curator.photoShows: Seated_Cable_Rows and Elevated_Cable_Rows: seated low-pulley rows with a close neutral-grip V-handle. Low_Pulley_Row_To_Neck: seated low-pulley row with a rope pulled to the neck, elbows high. Cable_Rope_Rear-Delt_Rows: standing rope face pull from a mid/high pulley.
curator.why: No source shows a seated cable row with a wide straight or lat bar. Every seated cable row in the source uses a V-handle (already rejected for this exercise) or a rope. Seated_One-arm_Cable_Pulley_Rows is a one-arm single-handle row. No other cable row variant exists in names.txt.

curator.photoShows: Cable_Incline_Pushdown: seated back on an upright incline bench, facing away from a high pulley, with a straight bar. Frame 0 has the arms straight overhead; frame 1 has the bar pulled to the lower chest with the elbows bent about 90 degrees, so it looks like a bent-arm pulldown. Rope_Straight-Arm_Pulldown: standing with a slight hip hinge and a high-pulley rope, arms going straight from shoulder height down to the thighs. Straight-Arm_Pulldown: standing upright, wide bar, straight arms from shoulder height to the thighs.
curator.why: The app lists 'Cable Pullover' (#63) separately from 'Straight-Arm Cable Pulldown' (#62), and #62 already uses the Straight-Arm_Pulldown photo. That suggests #63 is the classic lying cable pullover: supine on a flat bench, arms nearly straight, arcing from behind the head to over the chest. No source shows that. The incline-bench candidate fails on two counts: the bench is a steep incline rather than flat, and the elbows bend and the bar is pulled to the chest. The standing rope and bar straight-arm pulldowns would teach a standing body position for what is probably a lying exercise. Near miss: if the app means the standing 'cable pullover' (the rope straight-arm pulldown), Rope_Straight-Arm_Pulldown would fit, with frame 0 as the start. With the app separating the two names, that is too uncertain to propose.

curator.photoShows: The source has no pullover machine. The only pullovers are free-weight versions (Bent-Arm_Barbell_Pullover, Bent-Arm_Dumbbell_Pullover, Straight-Arm_Dumbbell_Pullover, Wide-Grip_Decline_Barbell_Pullover, Front_Raise_And_Pullover), and the machine lat and back exercises are rows (Leverage_Iso_Row, Leverage_High_Row, Lying_T-Bar_Row, Smith_Machine_Bent_Over_Row).
curator.why: A machine pullover is a seated, selectorized pullover machine where the arms or elbows press against pads that arc from overhead down to the torso. No source exercise uses that implement or movement. A dumbbell or barbell pullover is a different implement and a supine body position, and a machine row is a different movement. I did not view these frames because none of them can match on implement and pattern.

curator.photoShows: Bodyweight pull-up on a fixed pull-up bar, two arms, pronated (palms forward) grip slightly wider than shoulders, seen from behind. Frame 0: dead hang with arms fully extended and knees slightly bent. Frame 1: pulled up with the bar at upper-chest height.
curator.why: This is the standard bodyweight pull-up: overhand grip on a bar, two arms, vertical pull from a hang to chin over the bar. The generic app name maps to this standard version. Chin-Up uses a supinated grip, and Wide-Grip Rear Pull-Up goes behind the neck, so Pullups is the clearest true match.

reviewers.reason: I looked at both frames. The set-up matches a standard Pull-Up: an athlete with no added load (no belt, chain, plate or vest) hangs from a fixed pull-up bar on a rack, seen from behind. He uses both arms with an overhand grip: the backs of his gloved hands face the camera, so his palms face away from him. His hands are on the straight part of the bar just inside the bends, a little wider than his shoulders. There is no band, no machine, no neutral or V-handle, and the grip is neither underhand nor behind the neck. His feet are off the floor with knees bent, which is a normal free hang. In frame 0 he is in a dead hang with elbows straight. In frame 1 his elbows are fully bent, his head is above the bar and the bar is at upper-chest or collarbone height. That is a full vertical pull with the torso staying upright. The source's own text calls for a pronated grip, arms fully extended to start, and pulling until the bar touches the upper chest, and the photos show exactly that. Anyone copying these two frames would do a standard pull-up.

I viewed both frames, and they show a standard bodyweight pull-up from behind with no added load. The athlete hangs from a fixed overhead pull-up bar on a rack, using both arms and an overhand grip: the backs of his gloved hands face the camera, and his hands are about shoulder width or a little wider. In frame 0 he hangs with his arms fully straight, knees bent and ankles crossed, and his feet are off the floor. In frame 1 he has pulled straight up so his head is over the bar and his upper back is level with it. His elbows have bent and moved down to his sides, and his shoulder blades are drawn down and together. This is a vertical pull through full range, from straight arms to chin over the bar. It is not a chin-up (the grip is not underhand), not an isometric hold, not a scapular pull-up (his elbows bend fully) and not a weighted or assisted version. Someone copying these two frames would do the app's generic Pull-Up.

curator.photoShows: Closest candidate is Weighted_Pull_Ups: a dip belt with a chain and a plate hanging between the legs, on a power-tower's angled handles. The grip is wide and PRONATED (palms facing forward), so it is a weighted pull-up. Chin-Up shows a supinated close grip with no load.
curator.why: A chin-up is defined by the supinated (underhand) grip. The only loaded photo (Weighted_Pull_Ups) is a wide overhand pull-up, so it shows a different grip and movement. The only chin-up photo (Chin-Up) has no belt or load, which is the flaw already rejected by hand. No source photo shows an underhand chin-up with added weight.

curator.photoShows: Mixed_Grip_Chin: athlete faces the bar square-on, hands about shoulder width apart, one overhand and one underhand. V-Bar_Pullup: a V-handle draped over the bar, with a close neutral grip on the handle rather than the bar. Side_To_Side_Chins: wide overhand grip, body shifted toward one hand.
curator.why: In a commando pull-up the body is turned side-on to the bar, both hands grip the bar close together one in front of the other, and the head clears alternate sides of the bar. Mixed_Grip_Chin is facing the bar with shoulder-width hands, not side-on. V-Bar_Pullup uses a V-handle attachment and does not alternate sides. Side_To_Side_Chins uses a wide grip facing the bar. None of them shows the commando grip or path.

curator.photoShows: Side_To_Side_Chins: wide overhand grip. Frame 0 is a hang. In frame 1 the body is pulled up and shifted toward the right hand, but BOTH elbows are deeply bent.
curator.why: An archer pull-up keeps the non-working arm nearly straight and extended out to the side while the other arm pulls. In Side_To_Side_Chins both arms flex and the torso only leans to one side, which is a lateral-lean wide pull-up, not an archer. The standard Pullups photo is the base exercise, which the rules forbid for a named variation. No source shows one arm locked straight.

curator.photoShows: Gorilla_Chin_Crunch: overhand-grip hang with knees bent about 90 degrees and shins hanging down, then a pull-up with the knees tucked to the chest. Pullups: legs hang down with slightly bent knees.
curator.why: An L-sit pull-up holds both legs straight and horizontal (hips flexed to 90 degrees, knees locked) for the whole pull. Gorilla_Chin_Crunch uses bent knees tucked dynamically, so the trunk position and abdominal demand differ. Pullups has the legs hanging. Hanging_Leg_Raise and Hanging_Pike are leg raises with no pull-up. No source shows a pull-up with the legs held straight in an L.

curator.photoShows: Inverted_Row: bar in a rack, heels on the floor. Inverted_Row_with_Straps: TRX straps, heels on the floor. Suspended_Row: rings at a steep standing lean, feet on the floor. Bodyweight_Mid_Row: hanging upside down from a pull-up bar with legs hooked over it, nearly vertical.
curator.why: None of the sources shows the feet on a bench or box with the body horizontal. Inverted_Row (feet on floor) was already rejected for exactly that reason. The straps and rings versions also have feet on the floor and use a different implement. Bodyweight_Mid_Row is an inverted hang with the legs over the bar, a different movement and body position.

curator.photoShows: One_Arm_Chin-Up: one hand grips the pull-up bar directly and the other holds a small towel draped over the bar, close beside it. It is an asymmetric one-arm chin-up progression.
curator.why: A towel pull-up hangs from towels looped over the bar with BOTH hands gripping the towels, as a grip-strength variation. The only towel photo has one hand on the bar and only the other on a towel, so the attachment and grip demand differ, and it is a uneven one-arm progression rather than a two-hand towel pull. Standing_Towel_Triceps_Extension is unrelated. No source shows a two-hand towel pull-up.

curator.photoShows: Trap_Bar_Deadlift: a hex/trap bar with the athlete squatting down to the floor handles (frame 0), then standing tall at lockout (frame 1). This is a full deadlift with no shrug.
curator.why: The source has no trap-bar shrug. Trap_Bar_Deadlift uses the right implement but shows a deadlift (hips and knees extend from the floor), not scapular elevation. Barbell_Shrug, Dumbbell_Shrug, Cable_Shrugs and the machine shrugs show the right movement with the wrong implement. A barbell or dumbbell shrug is not a trap-bar shrug.

curator.photoShows: Dumbbells in both hands. The athlete lies chest-down on a steep incline bench with feet on the floor and arms straight, hanging vertically (frame 0). In frame 1 the shoulder blades are drawn up and back and both dumbbells rise a few inches with the arms still straight. Two-arm, no elbow bend.
curator.why: This is the chest-supported incline dumbbell shrug: dumbbells, prone on an incline bench, two arms, straight arms, and only the shoulder girdle moves the weights. The source describes the action as squeezing the shoulder blades together (an up-and-back shrug), which is how the incline shrug is coached and looks the same in still frames. It is medium rather than high only because the source text stresses retraction while the app labels the movement scapular elevation. Dumbbell_Incline_Shoulder_Raise was rejected: it is a supine protraction movement with the dumbbells pressed overhead, not a shrug.

reviewers.reason: I viewed both frames, plus an enlarged crop of the shoulders. The athlete holds a dumbbell in each hand and lies chest-down on a steep incline bench, roughly 45 degrees, with feet on the floor. That is exactly how an incline dumbbell shrug is set up: two dumbbells, both arms, chest supported, no extra surface. In frame 0 the arms hang straight down. In frame 1 the elbows are still locked and both dumbbells have risen about 40px straight up, about a hand's height, while the shoulder line rises and draws back. There is no elbow bend, so it is not a row. The source text cues 'squeeze shoulder blades together' (retraction), but from this angle the photos show the usual up-and-back incline-shrug path, and nothing visible would lead someone to a different movement. I found no other incline or chest-supported shrug source to prefer. Copying the frames gives a chest-supported incline dumbbell shrug.

I viewed both frames. He holds a dumbbell in each hand and lies chest-down on a steep incline bench (about 45-60 degrees) with feet on the floor. In frame 0 the arms hang straight down and relaxed. In frame 1 the arms stay straight, both dumbbells rise a few inches, and a zoomed crop shows the shoulders lifting toward the ears with the upper traps bunched and the head sitting lower between the shoulders. That is shoulder-blade elevation with some retraction: a chest-supported incline shrug. It is not a row, because the elbows never bend, and not a rear-delt raise, because the arms stay vertical. The source's text cues 'squeeze the shoulder blades together', but the photos clearly show an up-and-back shrug, which is how the incline dumbbell shrug is normally coached. Implement (two dumbbells), laterality (both arms), body position (prone, incline, supported) and movement all match.

curator.photoShows: Cable, low pulley, single D-handle in one hand. The athlete stands hinged forward with the torso near parallel to the floor and knees soft, the free hand on the thigh. The working arm hangs across the body toward the pulley (frame 0), then sweeps out to the side to shoulder height with a slightly bent elbow (frame 1). One arm only.
curator.why: It is a one-arm cable reverse (rear-delt) fly: cable, single handle, single arm, straight-arm horizontal abduction across and away from the body. This fixes the earlier rejection, where Cable_Rear_Delt_Fly was two-arm. It is medium rather than high because the photo shows the bent-over, low-pulley version, while some coaches teach the single-arm cable rear-delt fly standing upright with the pulley at shoulder height. The app name does not specify the position, and relative to the torso the movement is the same. Standing_Low-Pulley_Deltoid_Raise was rejected: it is upright and raises the arm laterally in the frontal plane, so it is a side lateral raise, not a rear-delt fly.

reviewers.reason: Both frames show a cable from a low pulley with a single stirrup or D-handle, clipped on with a carabiner, in the right hand only. The left hand rests on the thigh, so this is truly single-arm, which fixes the earlier rejection of a two-arm photo. The athlete stands hinged forward with knees bent. In frame 0 the working arm hangs across the midline, with the cable running from the pulley on his left side across the body to his right hand. In frame 1 the arm sweeps out to the side, perpendicular to the hinged torso and level with the shoulder line, with the elbow slightly bent. That is horizontal abduction against the cable, a rear-delt fly path and not a front or lateral raise. The implement (cable), handle (single handle), laterality (one arm) and movement pattern (reverse fly) all match. The app name does not specify upright versus bent-over, and the bent-over low-pulley cross-body version is a standard way to do a single-arm cable rear-delt fly. Note that this differs in body position from the upright high-pulley two-arm Cable_Rear_Delt_Fly photo, but nothing in the name rules it out.

I viewed both frames. It is a cable from a low pulley, with a single D-handle in his right hand only. The pulley sits on his opposite side, so the cable crosses in front of his body. He stands hinged well forward at the hips (roughly 45-60 degrees, not fully parallel) with knees soft and the free hand on his left thigh. In frame 0 the working arm hangs in front, across the body, with a slight elbow bend. In frame 1 the same arm has swept out to the side to shoulder height, almost straight, with the cable crossing his body. Raising the arm sideways while bent over is horizontal abduction, which works the rear delt: the standard single-arm cross-body cable rear-delt raise or fly. This one-arm source fixes the earlier rejection, which was for a two-arm photo. Implement, handle, laterality and movement all match. The hinge is a little less than parallel, but well within normal coaching for this exercise.

curator.photoShows: Closest is Dumbbell_Scaption: standing, two dumbbells, thumbs up, arms raised in the scapular plane from the sides (frame 0) to just above shoulder height (frame 1), forming a wide V or T. The arms never reach the overhead Y.

curator.photoShows: Closest is Straight_Raises_on_Incline_Bench: prone on an incline bench, a barbell held with an overhand, roughly shoulder-width grip hangs down (frame 0), then is raised straight in front of the head (frame 1). The arms stay parallel (an I), fixed by the bar.
curator.why: The prone position is right, but the movement is a barbell front raise with the arms parallel. A barbell cannot make a Y, so this is a prone I-raise, not a Y-raise. The other prone raises (Dumbbell_Lying_Rear_Lateral_Raise, Reverse_Flyes, Lying_Rear_Delt_Raise) finish in a T at shoulder level, not a Y overhead. Superman is a lower-back extension. curator.photoShows: Two light dumbbells, chest-down on a shallow (about 15 degree) incline bench, shot from the front. Arms hang straight below the bench with a neutral grip (frame 0), then are raised straight out to the sides to shoulder level, forming a clear T with the shoulder blades retracted (frame 1). Two-arm, arms nearly straight.
curator.why: It matches the prone T-raise on implement (light free weights), position (prone, chest supported, near horizontal), laterality (both arms), and pattern (straight-arm horizontal abduction to a T at shoulder height). It is medium rather than high because the source frames it as a rear-delt raise with a neutral-to-palms-down grip, while the T-raise is often cued thumbs up; that grip detail does not change the movement. Reverse_Flyes (steeper incline, slightly bent elbows) and Reverse_Flyes_With_External_Rotation (adds a forearm rotation from pronated to thumbs up) also reach a T but are less clean. Lying_Rear_Delt_Raise (flat bench) is valid but shot from the side, so the T is hard to read, and its frame 0 is the top. The single-arm versions were excluded on laterality.

reviewers.reason: Both frames, viewed and enlarged, show two light dumbbells (15 lb). The athlete's chest is down on an incline bench, he straddles it with feet on the floor, and the shot is from the front. It is two-arm, prone and chest-supported. In frame 0 the arms hang straight below the bench. In frame 1 both arms are lifted straight out to the sides to shoulder height, perpendicular to the torso, elbows almost straight, forming a clear T. That matches the prone T-raise plane (horizontal abduction at 90 degrees) and its range. The dumbbell end plates face the camera in frame 1, so the palms face down. Many coaches cue the T-raise with thumbs up instead, but the rules do not require grip orientation to match, and the path, plane, laterality, body position and implement all do. Copying the frames gives a dumbbell prone T-raise. This photo overlaps with the Chest-Supported Rear-Delt Raise, which is allowed.

I viewed both frames, which are shot from the front. He lies chest-down on a shallow-incline bench holding two dumbbells (marked 15). In frame 0 both arms hang straight below the bench. In frame 1 both arms are raised almost straight out to the sides to shoulder level, at right angles to the torso, making a clear T with the shoulder blades squeezed together. The dumbbell ends face the camera in the top position, so the palms face the floor. That is the prone horizontal-abduction pattern of the T in Y-T-W-I. Arms near straight, a T path and a prone, supported position mean someone copying these frames does a prone T-raise, not a bent-elbow rear-delt row or fly. Load matches the app's free-weights label, and both arms work at once. Thumbs-up is a common cue for the T, but hand orientation is a grip detail within the same named exercise and doesn't change the movement.

curator.photoShows: Closest photos show prone or chest-supported dumbbell raises with straight arms into a T: Lying_Rear_Delt_Raise (flat bench, straight-arm T), Dumbbell_Lying_Rear_Lateral_Raise (low incline, straight-arm T) and Reverse_Flyes_With_External_Rotation (30-degree incline, straight-arm T with external rotation). The athlete squeezes the shoulder blades down and back and rotates the forearms up and out so the arms form a W. curator.photoShows: Kettlebell_Seated_Press: a man sits on the floor with his legs spread wide in a straddle and presses one kettlebell from the shoulder (frame 0) to lockout (frame 1). The free arm is out to the side, with the hand near or on the floor for balance.

The photo is one arm with a kettlebell and straddled legs, and the free hand may be bracing on the floor. That differs from the standard version in laterality and implement, and possibly in support. curator.photoShows: Chin-Up: two arms, close grip on a pull-up station, back view. Frame 0 is a dead hang with arms straight; frame 1 pulls the head to bar level. It is a standard vertical chin-up. Gorilla_Chin_Crunch is an underhand chin-up combined with a knee tuck.

curator.photoShows: No source shows a dead hang held still as both frames. One_Handed_Hang: one arm on a high cable-station handle, feet on the floor, leaning sideways into a lat stretch. Scapular_Pull-Up: frame 0 is a two-arm overhand hang with knees bent; frame 1 shows the shoulder blades pulled down and the body raised a few inches. Hanging_Pike: frame 0 is a clean two-arm hang; frame 1 is a toes-to-bar pike. Chin-Up and Gorilla_Chin_Crunch: frame 1 pulls up to the bar.

In every candidate only frame 0 is a hang, and frame 1 shows a different movement (scapular pull-up, pike, chin-up). Someone copying the pair would do that movement instead of hanging. One_Handed_Hang is one-armed, keeps the feet on the floor and is a stretch. The closest is Scapular_Pull-Up, but its frame 1 is a scapular pull-up, which the app lists as its own exercise (#79).

curator.photoShows: The only source with a towel on a bar is One_Arm_Chin-Up. One hand grips the bar and the other holds a towel looped over it. Frame 0 hangs and frame 1 pulls up to chin height, knees bent. No source shows a two-hand towel grip held still.

One_Arm_Chin-Up has one hand on the bar and one on a towel, and its frame 1 is a pull-up, not a hang. No other source mentions a towel on a hanging exercise. Plain dead-hang frames (Scapular_Pull-Up, Hanging_Pike frame 0) have no towel and are not dead hangs either (see #143).

curator.photoShows: Farmers_Walk: frame 0 athlete bent over gripping two farmer's-walk handles on the ground; frame 1 upright carrying them at his sides mid-stride (one foot ahead), walking toward camera. Dumbbell_Shrug: standing with dumbbells at sides, frame 1 shoulders shrugged. Plate_Pinch: one hand pinching two plates at the side. Standing_Olympic_Plate_Hand_Squeeze: one hand rolling a plate by its rim with the fingers.
curator.why: Farmer Hold is a static grip hold: stand still holding heavy implements at your sides. Farmer's Walk is the loaded-carry version; its frame 1 clearly shows walking, so someone copying it would carry, not hold. The name 'Hold' is what sets the exercise apart from the walk, so this is the base exercise standing in for a named variation. Dumbbell Shrug's frame 0 looks like the hold position, but frame 1 is a shrug, so the pair teaches shrugging. Plate Pinch and the plate squeeze use a one-hand pinch or finger grip on plates, not a two-hand farmer hold. No source shows a static two-hand farmer hold.

curator.photoShows: Body_Tricep_Press: hands on a bar set at chest height in a rack, body leaning on straight arms with feet together (frame 0). The elbows then flex so the head drops below the bar (frame 1). Heavy chains are draped around the neck and over the shoulders in BOTH frames. Body-Up: frame 0 is a forearm plank on the floor; frame 1 is pressed up onto the hands with arms straight.
curator.why: Body_Tricep_Press is exactly the movement (the standard bar 'bodyweight skull crusher'), but the photos show visible added load: chains over the shoulders. The rule says 'Bodyweight' must be unloaded, so it is a near miss and is rejected. A reviewer who accepts the chains could use it, and its frame 0 (arms extended) is the rep start. Body-Up is unloaded, but it is the floor forearm-to-hands 'sphinx/tiger' variation, a different set-up from the bar/ledge bodyweight triceps extension. The app lists 'Free weights', which also suggests a bar is used. Standing_Towel_Triceps_Extension is partner-resisted with a towel overhead, not bodyweight-loaded.

curator.photoShows: No pendulum-squat machine in the source. Hack_Squat: linear-sled hack squat machine, shoulders under pads, two legs, lockout then bottom. Lying_Machine_Squat: reclined 'lying squat' machine, feet on an angled footplate, pressing upward like a leg press. Barbell_Hack_Squat: standing with a free barbell held behind the legs.
curator.why: A pendulum squat uses a dedicated machine whose shoulder-pad carriage swings on a pivot arc. The source has no such machine. The hack squat (linear sled), the lying machine squat (reclined press-style machine) and the barbell hack squat (barbell behind the legs) are different implements with a different movement path. Searches for 'pendulum' and 'squat machine' found nothing closer.

curator.photoShows: Leg_Press: 45-degree plate-loaded leg press with both feet on the platform, legs extended in frame 0 and bent in frame 1. Narrow_Stance_Leg_Press: the same machine with both feet close together. Smith_Machine_Leg_Press: lying on the floor under a Smith bar with both feet pressing it.
curator.why: Every leg-press photo in the source shows both legs pressing. The app exercise is single-leg, so a two-leg photo breaks the laterality rule. No source exercise shows a one-leg press (searched 'leg press', 'single', 'one leg'). Single-Leg_Leg_Extension is a different movement.

curator.photoShows: Split_Squat_with_Dumbbells: rear foot on a flat bench (Bulgarian, rear-foot elevated), dumbbells at the sides. Smith_Single-Leg_Split_Squat: rear foot on a bench under a Smith bar. Suspended_Split_Squat: rear foot in a gymnastic ring or strap. Split_Squats: bodyweight jumping split on the floor. Elevated_Back_Lunge: frame 0 stands with both feet on a plate, frame 1 has the front foot on the plate and the rear knee near the floor after stepping back.
curator.why: The split squats in the source all elevate the REAR foot (bench or strap) or keep both feet on the floor; none elevates the front foot. Elevated_Back_Lunge does show front foot on a plate at the bottom (frame 1). Its frame 0, though, is both feet together on the plate, so the athlete steps back into a reverse lunge each rep instead of holding a fixed split stance. Someone copying those frames would perform a deficit reverse lunge, not a split squat.

curator.photoShows: Barbell on the upper back. Frame 0: standing tall with both feet together on a raised weight plate (the deficit). Frame 1: one foot still on the plate, the other leg stepped back to the floor, rear knee lowered near the floor in a deep lunge.
curator.why: This is a deficit reverse lunge. The source instructions say: stand on a short raised platform, step backwards with one leg, descend until the knee touches the floor, then return all the way to the platform. The photos show a raised start surface, a backward step down to a lower floor, single-leg loading and a full knee-dominant range. The app name does not specify an implement, so the barbell is acceptable under 'Free weights'. Dumbbell_Rear_Lunge was rejected because it is the floor version with no deficit.

reviewers.reason: I viewed both frames. Frame 0: the athlete stands tall with both feet together on a single bumper plate on a wooden platform, with a barbell racked across the upper back. Frame 1: the front foot is still on the plate, the other leg has stepped back down to the floor behind him, and he is in a deep split with the rear knee lowered close to the floor and the torso upright. The front foot raised above the floor is the deficit, so this is a backward (reverse) lunge from a deficit. Every set-up point agrees: the barbell is a free weight, and the app name names no implement, so the standard loaded version is acceptable. It is one leg working (unilateral) and stepping back, not forward. The working foot is raised on the deficit and the rear foot goes to the floor. The bar looks lightly loaded or empty, but the name does not call for a specific load. The plate is a fairly small deficit, a few inches high, but it is clearly raised. Someone copying these two frames would perform a deficit reverse lunge.

I viewed both frames. Frame 0: the athlete stands upright with a barbell across the upper back and both feet together on a bumper plate, which raises him a few inches (the deficit). Frame 1: the front (working) foot stays on the plate while the other leg has stepped backward down to the lower floor. The front knee and hip are flexed, the torso is upright and the rear knee drops toward the floor. That is a reverse lunge in the sagittal plane: the rear foot steps back and the hips descend vertically, with the working foot raised above where the rear foot lands. This raised front foot is exactly what makes it a deficit reverse lunge. It is not a forward lunge, a rear-foot-elevated split squat (the rear foot is not raised) or a static split squat (frame 0 shows the feet together, so the leg steps back). The app name does not specify an implement and the equipment field is 'Free weights', so a barbell back load fits. Laterality, stance and the knee-dominant pattern all match. Someone copying these frames would perform a deficit reverse lunge.

curator.photoShows: Dumbbell_Step_Ups: frame 0 stands on top of a bench, frame 1 steps down with one foot on the bench and dumbbells at the sides, flat-footed. Barbell_Step_Ups: low box, frame 0 one foot on the box with the other on the floor, frame 1 standing on the box with the opposite knee driven up. Step-up_with_Knee_Raise: bodyweight, standing on one leg with the other knee raised high.
curator.why: In a Peterson step-up you stand on a low step with the working heel raised and the knee driven forward over the toes, then extend that knee to lift the body; it is a VMO-focused, short-range movement. All source step-ups are ordinary flat-foot step-ups (some with a knee drive). None shows the heel-raised, knee-forward Peterson technique. Under the rules, the base step-up does not stand in for this named variation.

curator.photoShows: Narrow_Stance_Squats: barbell back squat, feet a few inches apart, heels flat on the floor, standing then deep squat. Weighted_Sissy_Squat: one hand on a rack upright, a plate held to the chest, squatting with knees forward, heels on the floor.
curator.why: A cyclist squat is a narrow-stance squat with the heels raised on a wedge or plates, which pushes the knees well forward to load the quads. No source exercise shows heel elevation; an instructions search for heels on, raised or elevated, wedges or plates under the feet found nothing for squats. Narrow_Stance_Squats lacks the heel elevation that defines the exercise. The sissy squat is a different movement, a backward lean with the hips kept extended.

The source has no such exercise; searches for 'spanish', band-behind-knee wording and the band/squat variants found none. Squats_-_With_Bands uses the band as resistance from under the feet, which is a different setup and loading.

curator.photoShows: Kettlebell_Pistol_Squat: standing, then a full-depth free-standing pistol holding a kettlebell by the horns, with no support. Smith_Machine_Pistol_Squat: loaded barbell on the back in a Smith machine, standing, then a deep single-leg squat with the free leg extended forward. Single-Leg_High_Box_Squat: man holding a band hung from a rack, standing on a high box on one leg, then stepping down with one foot on the box.
curator.why: The source has no pistol squat assisted by a hand support (TRX, band, pole or door frame). The kettlebell pistol is an unassisted, loaded pistol. The Smith-machine pistol carries a barbell load and is machine-guided. Both are a different variation from a bodyweight assisted pistol. Single-Leg_High_Box_Squat does use a band for balance, but it is a single-leg step-up and step-down onto a high box, not a floor pistol with the free leg held out in front. Matching the base pistol to a named assisted variation is not acceptable.

curator.photoShows: Natural_Glute_Ham_Raise: kneeling upright on a preacher-type bench with ankles hooked under the pad (frame 0), then lowered all the way to the floor and catching himself with both hands in a push-up position (frame 1). No band or partner, so the lowering is unassisted. Floor_Glute-Ham_Raise: kneeling upright on the floor while a partner holds his ankles, arms crossed (frame 0), then leaning partway forward from the knees with no hands on the floor and no band (frame 1). Glute_Ham_Raise: GHD machine, from fully flexed at the hips to upright.
curator.why: The source has only the unassisted Nordic, and it is already used for app #192 Nordic Hamstring Curl (Natural_Glute_Ham_Raise). No source shows the assistance that defines this variation: no band around the chest, no box or partner helping, no hand push-off during the lowering. The partner in Floor_Glute-Ham_Raise only anchors the feet, which is the standard Nordic set-up, not assistance. In Natural_Glute_Ham_Raise frame 1 the hands only catch the body at the bottom of a full Nordic. Glute_Ham_Raise is a GHD machine exercise with a different set-up. Using the base exercise for a named variation is not allowed.

curator.photoShows: Platform_Hamstring_Slides: lying on his back on a wooden floor with the legs straight and a towel under a heel (frame 0), then knees bent with the heel slid toward the buttocks on the towel (frame 1). Hips and back stay flat on the floor throughout, with no bridge. The source describes a single-leg version with the other leg straight.
curator.why: A slider hamstring curl is done with the hips bridged off the floor. The heels slide out and back in while the hips stay extended, which is what loads the hamstrings (the same set-up as Ball_Leg_Curl, but on sliders). This source photo is a heel slide with the hips on the floor. There is no bridge or hip extension, so the hamstrings barely work against gravity. Someone copying it would do a mobility-style heel slide, not the app's exercise. Ball_Leg_Curl uses a stability ball, a different implement, and is already app #197. No other slider or towel curl exists in the source.

curator.photoShows: Barbell held in the hands with an overhand grip, standing with feet about hip width. Frame 0: bent at the hips, hips pushed back, knees slightly bent, back flat, bar just below the knees. Frame 1: standing tall with the bar at the thighs. Both arms, both legs, free-standing.
curator.why: The app name is generic, and the standard barbell hip hinge is this pattern: bar in the hands, soft knees, hips driven back and forward. The secondary muscles listed (lowerBack, forearms, abs) also point to a bar held in the hands, as here, rather than on the back as in Good_Morning. Implement (barbell), laterality (two-arm, two-leg), body position (standing) and movement (hinge with soft knees) all agree. Stiff-Legged_Barbell_Deadlift shows a similar hinge, but its bottom frame has more knee bend and the bar nearer the floor, so the RDL photo is the clearer one.
