reviewers.reason: I viewed both frames. The implement is a cable from a pulley station to her side, with a chain attachment held in both hands clasped together. She stands with feet about hip-width apart and knees soft, square to the front, with no bench or kneeling. Frame 0 has the clasped hands at mid-chest. In frame 1 both arms are pressed straight out in front of the sternum while the cable pulls from the side, and the trunk does not rotate. That is the anti-rotation press-out. The app's own movementSupport.ts says a cable press-out is an anti-rotation press 'like the Pallof press', and the app's Pallof Press (#249) already uses this photo. The 'unilateral' quality fits the offset, one-sided cable load, and the name asks for no single-arm hold. One small point: the cable runs down to a low pulley rather than one at chest height. The source instructions allow that ('a low pulley will suffice') and the app name sets no pulley height, so someone copying these frames still performs a cable press-out.

I viewed both frames. Frame 0: she stands with feet about hip-width and knees soft, both hands clasped on a chain attachment held against mid-chest. The cable runs sideways and down to the tower's pulley on her side. Frame 1: both arms are pressed straight out in front of the sternum. The chain still angles away to her side and low, and her trunk faces forward with no rotation. That is the Pallof press: a straight-out press against a sideways cable pull, resisted by bracing, which makes it an anti-rotation press rather than a chest press. The app defines it the same way. Its movementSupport.ts says 'A cable press-out is an anti-rotation press for the trunk, like the Pallof press, not a cable chest or shoulder press', and its movement field is 'Anti-rotation press'. Primary abs/obliques also fit. The 'unilateral' quality is satisfied by the one-sided cable load, and the name implies no single-arm version. The implement (cable), stance (standing) and laterality (two hands on one attachment) all match. The pulley is set low rather than at shoulder height, which adds a slight diagonal to the pull. The source allows that ('a low pulley will suffice'), and it is the same exercise. This same photo is already used for the app's #249 Pallof Press.

curator.photoShows: Standing in a staggered stance between two high (above-head) pulleys, with a single D-handle in each hand and a slight forward lean. Frame 0: both arms out wide at about shoulder level with slight elbow bend, the cables running down from the high pulleys. Frame 1: both hands swept together in front of the lower chest and upper abdomen. This is a two-arm fly that moves forward and down (high-to-low).
curator.why: The app's group is Sport Transfer, the movement is 'Diagonal push', and abs and bracing appear as secondaries. Together these indicate the standing high-to-low cable fly, which coaches commonly call the decline cable fly (its counterpart, Cable Incline Fly, is the low-to-high fly). The high-pulley Cable_Crossover agrees on implement (cable, single handles), laterality (two arms together), position (standing) and pattern (a fly arc from high and wide to low in front). Medium confidence for two reasons. First, the finish is at lower-chest height rather than waist height, a modest decline. Second, a reader could take 'decline fly' to mean a decline-bench cable fly, which the source lacks. Alternative: Cable_Iron_Cross photos show the same high-pulley fly from a T to hands meeting in front of the hips, an even steeper decline arc. But that source's name and text describe pulling the arms to the sides (an iron cross), so I preferred the canonical crossover. I rejected Single-Arm_Cable_Crossover (single arm at a time), Flat_Bench_Cable_Flyes and Incline_Cable_Flye (on a bench, low pulleys) and Low_Cable_Crossover (low-to-high, the opposite angle).

reviewers.reason: I viewed both frames. He stands in a split/staggered stance between two cable towers, with a D-handle in each hand attached to pulleys set above head height, and leans forward slightly. There is no bench. Both arms work together, which suits a name that does not say single-arm. In frame 0 the arms are spread wide at about shoulder height with soft elbows, and the cables run up and out to the high pulleys. In frame 1 the hands have swept together in front of the lower sternum and upper abdomen, so they finish below where they started, against a pull coming from above. That is the high-to-low (decline-angle) cable fly as coaches normally define a standing 'decline cable fly', and it fits the app's 'Diagonal push' movement label. The app's own 'High-to-Low Cable Fly' (#20) already uses this photo. Implement, handles, laterality, stance and the fly pattern (not a press) all match. The one possible reading against it would be a fly on a decline bench, which the name does not require and the 'Diagonal push' label argues against.

I viewed both frames. Frame 0: he stands in a staggered stance between two cable towers, one D-handle in each hand. His arms are out to the sides at about shoulder height with soft elbows, and the cables run down to his hands from the top pulleys. Frame 1: the hands come together in front of the lower chest and upper abdomen. The upper arms have swept down from horizontal toward the sides of the torso, against cables that still pull from above. The motion is a fly (an arc with elbows held soft, not a press) on a high-to-low, downward-diagonal path toward the lower torso. That fits the app's definition: movement 'Diagonal push', cue 'low-angle pushing capacity', in the standing Sport Transfer group. Its counterpart 'Cable Incline Fly' is also 'Diagonal push', with the cue 'upward arm-path capacity', so the app names these by arm path. The implement (cable, two single handles), laterality (two arms at once) and position (standing, slight forward lean) are all consistent. Caveats: the arms start only at shoulder height, not above, and the elbows bend a little more at the finish than ideal. The path still clearly descends from high pulleys, so copying it gives a high-to-low (decline-path) cable fly. Residual risk: if the app actually meant a cable fly lying on a decline bench, this standing photo would be the wrong body position. Nothing in the app's metadata says bench, and the existing #312 match used a bench photo only because the source had one. This photo is already the app's #20 High-to-Low Cable Fly, which is the same exercise.

curator.photoShows: Front_Cable_Raise: one-arm front raise to shoulder height. Standing_Low-Pulley_Deltoid_Raise: one-arm lateral raise across the body to shoulder height. Bent_Over_Low-Pulley_Side_Lateral: bent-over one-arm rear-delt raise. Dumbbell_Scaption: dumbbells raised in the scapular plane to shoulder height.
curator.why: A cable Y raise brings the arms up at about 30 degrees off the midline, usually to overhead, so the body makes a Y. The cables typically come from low pulleys. No cable photo shows this. The cable photos are a front raise, a lateral raise and a bent-over rear-delt raise, all stopping at shoulder height. Dumbbell_Scaption is the closest path, but it uses dumbbells instead of cables and stops at shoulder height instead of reaching a Y overhead.

curator.photoShows: Closest cable photo, Standing_Low-Pulley_Deltoid_Raise: a single-arm cable lateral raise, standing side-on to a low pulley with the handle crossing in front of the body and a pronated grip. The arm rises out to the side in the frontal plane to shoulder height. Frame 0 is the top and frame 1 the bottom. Front_Cable_Raise: a single-arm low-pulley front raise straight forward in the sagittal plane, palm down. Dumbbell_Scaption shows the right movement (thumbs-up raise about 30 degrees in front of the frontal plane) but with two dumbbells.
curator.why: Scaption is a thumbs-up raise in the scapular plane, about 30 degrees forward of the side. Neither cable source shows it: one is a frontal-plane lateral raise with a pronated, cross-body grip and the other a sagittal-plane front raise. Someone copying either would do a lateral or front raise, not scaption. The only true scaption photo (Dumbbell_Scaption) uses dumbbells, not a cable. No cable scaption or Y-raise exists in the source.

curator.photoShows: External_Rotation_with_Cable: standing, one arm, D-handle from a cable at elbow height. The elbow is pinned at the side with a pad and the arm at 0 degrees abduction. The forearm rotates from across the stomach (frame 0) out to the side (frame 1). Cuban_Press (by name and instructions, not viewed) is a dumbbell scarecrow rotation followed by a press.
curator.why: A Cuban rotation is external rotation with the upper arm raised to shoulder height (90/90 scarecrow), with the forearm rotating from pointing forward or down to vertical. The cable photo shows external rotation with the elbow at the side, which is a different position and loads different parts of the range. Cuban_Press is the wrong implement (dumbbells) and adds an overhead press. The source has no cable 90/90 or Cuban rotation.

curator.photoShows: Standing_Cable_Chest_Press: a two-arm press from chest-height pulleys with D-handles, from elbows bent at 90 degrees out to near-full extension with the hands drawn together. It is a bilateral elbow-extension chest press, with no visible reach or protraction past lockout and no punching stance.
curator.why: A serratus punch is a protraction-focused punch, usually one arm, that ends with the shoulder blade reaching forward past arm lockout. The only cable press photos are bilateral chest presses (standing, or seated for Cable_Chest_Press) that train pressing, not protraction. Laterality and movement emphasis both differ. The source has no cable punch or cable protraction exercise.

curator.photoShows: Closest candidate: Standing_Cable_Chest_Press shows a standing, two-arm press with both handles pressed straight forward at chest height. The torso does not rotate, the press is not single-arm and there is no punch path. The other cable presses are seated or on a bench and two-arm.
curator.why: The app's exercise is a single-arm, rotational, standing cable punch (qualities: power, rotation, unilateral). No source shows a single-arm cable punch with trunk rotation. Standing_Cable_Chest_Press is two-arm and has no rotation. Pallof presses are anti-rotation two-hand press-outs. Heavy_Bag_Thrust and the medicine-ball chest pushes are not cable. Using a two-arm press for a single-arm rotational punch is explicitly not acceptable.

curator.photoShows: Closest candidates: Incline_Cable_Chest_Press shows two arms pressing straight up from the chest on an incline bench, with no single arm and no across-the-body path. Incline_Cable_Flye shows a two-arm fly on an incline bench. Single-Arm_Cable_Crossover shows a standing, alternating single-arm fly from high pulleys, which is a fly (not a press) on a downward line.
curator.why: A press-around is a single-arm cable press that sweeps across the body toward the midline. The app's version is on an upward (incline) line with anti-rotation demand. No source photo shows a single-arm press-around, incline or otherwise. The incline cable press and incline fly are two-arm and use a different pattern (a straight press, or a fly). Single-Arm_Cable_Crossover is a fly on a high-to-low line. All of them fail on laterality, movement pattern or angle.

curator.photoShows: Closest candidate: Standing_Cable_Chest_Press shows a standing, two-arm press with chest-height pulleys. The frames are cropped at the hips, so no stance, and no front foot on a step or plate, is visible. Cable_Chest_Press is seated.
curator.why: The app's exercise needs a split stance with the front foot elevated on a step or plate while pressing a cable. No source shows that stance. Standing_Cable_Chest_Press's text only says the stance may be staggered, its photo does not show the feet at all, and nothing is elevated. A plain standing cable press is the base exercise, not this named stance variation.

curator.photoShows: Rear view of an athlete kneeling on the floor, sitting back toward the heels, in front of a high-pulley cable stack, with a rope attachment held in both hands. Frame 0: both arms fully extended straight overhead toward the pulley. Frame 1: the rope pulled down two-handed to head level, elbows driven down and out, shoulder blades retracted. This is a two-arm vertical pull from a high cable.
curator.why: Implement (cable, high pulley), body position (kneeling), laterality (two-arm, simultaneous) and pattern (vertical pull from arms overhead down toward the upper chest with the elbows driving down) all agree with a kneeling cable lat pulldown. The source calls it a 'high pulley row', but its own instructions and the photos show a pulldown toward the upper chest from a near-vertical cable line. The app name does not specify an attachment, so a rope is acceptable. Kneeling_Single-Arm_High_Pulley_Row was rejected because it is single-arm. Caveats behind medium confidence: the finish is at head or ear level with the elbows fairly wide rather than at the upper chest, and the athlete sits back on the heels rather than tall-kneeling.

reviewers.reason: I viewed both frames and enlarged them. Implement: a cable from a high pulley on a weight-stack tower, which is correct for a cable exercise. Attachment: a rope. The app name names no attachment, so a rope is acceptable for a generic kneeling cable lat pulldown. Laterality: both hands are on the rope at the same time, matching a two-arm exercise. Body position: both knees are on the floor and the hips sit back low toward the heels, facing the stack. That is kneeling, not standing or seated on a bench, and the name only says 'Kneeling', not half- or tall-kneeling. Load: the stack is pinned. Movement: in frame 0 both arms are fully extended almost straight overhead toward the pulley, which is a vertical line of pull. In frame 1 the elbows are driven down and out below shoulder height, the shoulder blades are visibly pulled down and back, and the hands sit at ear level beside the head. The head hides the middle of the rope, so the rope is in front of the face and this is not a behind-the-neck pull. This is a vertical pulldown, not a horizontal row, despite the source's name. The finish is a little short of a bar to the upper chest, which is normal for a rope that splits around the head. Someone copying these two frames would do a kneeling two-arm cable pulldown, which is the app exercise.

I viewed both frames (rear view). Implement: a cable stack with a high pulley and a split rope held in both hands. The name 'Kneeling Cable Lat Pulldown' doesn't call for any particular attachment, so the rope is acceptable. Laterality: both arms work at the same time. Position: both knees on the mat with the hips sitting back toward the heels. That counts as 'kneeling' and the name doesn't ask for tall-kneeling. The torso stays upright, so this is not a standing or seated machine pulldown. Movement: in frame 0 both arms are fully extended overhead and the rope runs nearly vertically to the pulley above. In frame 1 the hands have come down to ear height, the elbows are driven down and out to below shoulder height, and the shoulder blades are visibly pulled back and down (the lats are clearly contracted). The shoulder moves from overhead flexion to adduction in the frontal/scapular plane. That is a vertical pull, i.e. a pulldown. It is not a horizontal row, a face pull or a straight-arm pulldown, and the elbows bend in the expected way. Although the source is named a 'row', the athlete is right under the pulley, so the pull in the frames is vertical. The end range is a bit short of a bar touching the chest, but it is normal for a rope pulldown. No load or stance qualifier is needed. Someone copying these frames would do a two-arm kneeling cable lat pulldown with an upright, braced trunk, which matches the app's cue ('vertical pulling with organized trunk position'). No better kneeling pulldown source exists: the only other kneeling high-pulley pull is the single-arm version.

curator.photoShows: Low cable with a single handle. The athlete stands in a wide split stance, hinged well forward with the torso pitched steeply toward horizontal. He rows one arm (right) from fully extended with the shoulder reaching forward (frame 0) to the elbow drawn back and the handle at the lower ribs/hip (frame 1). The free hand hangs by the front knee.
curator.why: Every element the name specifies agrees: cable, single handle, one arm, bent-over hinged torso, horizontal row from a low pulley. The name gives no stance, so the split stance is acceptable. The supination twist in the source's instructions is a minor grip detail and does not change the movement. The alternatives fail on body position: Seated_One-arm_Cable_Pulley_Rows is seated upright, and Kneeling_Single-Arm_High_Pulley_Row is kneeling and pulls from a high pulley in a pulldown path. Confidence is medium because the source calls this a split-stance 'shotgun row' rather than a bent-over row, although the photos clearly show a bent-over torso.

reviewers.reason: I viewed both frames. The implement is a cable from a low floor pulley, with a single D-handle in one hand. The athlete rows with his right arm only and the left arm does not pull, so the laterality is single-arm. He stands in a wide split stance, left foot forward and right leg back. His torso is hinged steeply forward, well past 45 degrees and close to horizontal in frame 0, so this is a genuine bent-over position. He is not upright, kneeling or seated, and there is no chest support or bench. In frame 0 the right arm is fully extended toward the low pulley with the shoulder reaching forward. In frame 1 the elbow is drawn back past the torso and the handle sits at the lower ribs/hip. The free hand hangs by the front knee. The pull runs roughly perpendicular to the torso, which is a horizontal row and not a high or lat pull. That fits a cable single-arm bent-over row as a coach defines it, and the app name specifies no stance that the split stance would conflict with. The source asks for a supinating wrist turn, but frame 1 shows only a slight turn. That is minor and does not change the exercise. Someone copying these frames would perform a single-arm, bent-over, low-cable row.

I viewed both frames. The implement is a low cable with a single handle, which matches the Cable exercise and needs a one-hand attachment. Only one arm works: the other hand, wearing a wrist strap, hangs by the front knee in both frames. The athlete stands with a wide staggered (split) stance and a deep hip hinge, torso roughly 25-35 degrees above horizontal, so the position is clearly bent-over rather than upright, seated or kneeling. Frame 0 has the working arm fully extended toward the stack. Frame 1 has the elbow driven high behind the torso and the handle at the hip and lower ribs. That is a true single-arm row toward the hip (elbow flexion plus shoulder extension and scapular retraction), not a pulldown, a fly or a straight-arm pull. The arm path arcs from in front of the shoulder back to the hip, the lat-biased row that fits the lats/upperBack primaries. The app name does not specify a stance, and a staggered stance with the free hand near the knee is the standard set-up for this lift. One caveat on the movement: frame 0 shows a strong reach, with the working shoulder dropped forward and some upper-back rotation that opens up by frame 1. The source describes this as a protraction reach ('shoulder forward'). The torso stays hinged and does not rotate the whole trunk through the pull, so this is not a separate rotational-row exercise. Someone copying the frames would do a cable single-arm bent-over row, though the app's antiRotation cue (keep the shoulders square) should be stated in its text. I found no better source: Seated One-arm Cable Pulley Rows is seated and Kneeling Single-Arm High Pulley Row is kneeling with a high pulley.

curator.photoShows: Lying_T-Bar_Row: plate-loaded lever T-bar machine, chest on a pad. Dumbbell_Incline_Row: two dumbbells, chest on an incline bench. Seated_Cable_Rows: seated V-handle cable row with no chest pad.
curator.why: The source has no cable row with the chest supported. The chest-supported rows that exist use a lever machine (Lying_T-Bar_Row), dumbbells (Dumbbell_Incline_Row) or barbells (Lying_Cambered_Barbell_Row, Straight_Bar_Bench_Mid_Rows), so the implement is wrong. The cable rows are all free-torso seated, standing or kneeling rows.

curator.photoShows: Low_Pulley_Row_To_Neck: seated low-pulley rope row, arms extended (frame 0), then the rope pulled to the neck with the upper arms raised parallel to the floor and elbows flared high (frame 1). Cable_Rope_Rear-Delt_Rows: actually a standing rope face pull from a mid/high pulley, rope to the face.
curator.why: A standard rope cable row pulls the rope to the lower chest or upper abdomen with the elbows travelling back along the torso, a lat and upper-back row. The only rope rows in the source are a rear-delt/high row to the neck with the arms abducted to 90 degrees, which takes the lats largely out of the movement, and a standing face pull. Copying either would teach a high row or face pull, not the app's row; the app lists a separate 'Cable High Row' for that pattern. The remaining seated cable rows use a V-handle or a single handle, not a rope.

curator.photoShows: Cable_Shrugs: standing at a low pulley with a straight/cambered bar held overhand at the thighs, arms straight, shrugging the shoulders up (frame 0 low, frame 1 shoulders elevated). Bent_Over_Low-Pulley_Side_Lateral: bent over almost parallel to the floor, raising one arm out to the side to shoulder height (rear-delt horizontal abduction). Frame 0 is the bottom and frame 1 the top.
curator.why: A 'trap raise' as coaches use the term is a trap-3 or Y-raise: an arm raise diagonally overhead in line with the lower-trap fibres. The app's secondary muscles (rear delts, rotator cuff) support this reading. The cable shrug is a different movement (pure elevation with no arm raise), and the bent-over cable lateral is a rear-delt raise perpendicular to the torso, not a Y or trap-3 path. The app's movement label 'Scapular elevation' leans toward a shrug, but the name says 'raise', not 'shrug'. When in doubt this is not a match. No cable Y-raise or trap-3 raise exists in the source.

curator.photoShows: Upright_Cable_Row: standing at a low pulley with a cambered/straight bar, close overhand grip. The bar is pulled close to the body up to the chin with elbows high. Frame 0 is the top (bar at chin) and frame 1 the bottom (bar at thighs). The torso and legs stay still and upright throughout, which the instructions require ('keep your torso stationary').
curator.why: A high pull is an explosive pull driven by hip and knee extension, ending with the elbows high and wide. The app lists power and coordination, with glutes and quads as secondary muscles ('rapid whole-body arm-drive'). The only cable candidate is a strict, slow upright row with the torso held still and no lower-body drive. It is a close cousin, but someone copying the frames would do an upright row, not a high pull. Other high pulls in the source (Kettlebell_Sumo_High_Pull, barbell clean or snatch pulls) use the wrong implement.

curator.photoShows: Lying_Cable_Curl: lying flat on a floor mat, feet against the low-pulley frame, two-hand straight-bar curl to the chest. The incline curls in the source (Incline_Dumbbell_Curl, Barbell_Curls_Lying_Against_An_Incline) use dumbbells or a barbell, not a cable.
curator.why: Incline Cable Curl means lying back on an incline bench and curling from a low pulley (arms hanging behind the torso). The only lying cable curl is flat on the floor, which is a different body position and shoulder angle, and every incline curl in the source uses free weights. Body position and implement can't both be right in any one photo.

curator.photoShows: Concentration_Curls: seated on a bench, elbow braced on the inner thigh, one-arm DUMBBELL curl. Standing_One-Arm_Cable_Curl: standing upright, one-arm low-pulley curl with the upper arm at the side, no thigh brace.
curator.why: The concentration-curl photos (seated, standing, barbell) all use free weights, which the rules rule out for a cable exercise. The only single-arm cable curl is a standing upright curl with no elbow-on-thigh brace, so it isn't a concentration curl. No source shows a cable concentration curl.

curator.photoShows: Spider_Curl: chest against the vertical side of a preacher bench, arms hanging straight down, EZ-BAR curl. Cable_Preacher_Curl: seated with upper arms resting on the angled preacher pad, straight-bar curl from a low pulley.
curator.why: A spider curl has the chest supported and the arms hanging free and vertical, with no pad under the upper arms. The source spider curl uses an EZ bar, not a cable, and the cable preacher curl rests the upper arms on the preacher pad, which makes it a preacher curl. Neither is a cable spider curl.

curator.photoShows: Cross_Body_Hammer_Curl: standing, one-arm neutral-grip DUMBBELL curl across the body toward the opposite shoulder. Standing_One-Arm_Cable_Curl: standing, single-handle low-pulley curl with a supinated grip straight up to the same-side shoulder. Cable_Hammer_Curls_-_Rope_Attachment: standing facing the low pulley, two-hand rope hammer curl straight up.
curator.why: The only cross-body curl in the source uses a dumbbell, which isn't acceptable for a cable exercise. The single-arm cable curl goes straight up on the same side with a supinated grip, so it has neither the cross-body path nor the brachialis-focused neutral grip, and the rope hammer curl is two-arm and straight up. Nothing shows a cable curled across the body.

curator.photoShows: Closest candidates: Cable_One_Arm_Tricep_Extension shows a standing single-arm pushdown with a single handle and an underhand grip, with the elbow pinned at the side and the forearm moving straight down beside the hip. Standing_Low-Pulley_One-Arm_Triceps_Extension shows a single-arm overhead extension behind the head. Kneeling_Cable_Triceps_Extension shows a two-arm straight-bar overhead extension, kneeling with the upper arms on a bench.
curator.why: No source exercise shows a cross-body cable triceps extension, where the handle is taken from the opposite side and the elbow extends across or away from the body. The closest one, the single-arm pushdown, moves in a straight line down at the side. Copying it would give a single-arm pushdown, which the app already lists as #346 and which already uses that photo. The overhead and kneeling versions use a different plane and body position. The source instructions contain no cross-body triceps work.

curator.photoShows: No cable kickback exists in the source. The only triceps kickback is Tricep_Dumbbell_Kickback, which uses dumbbells. The cable triceps candidates I viewed (Cable_One_Arm_Tricep_Extension, Standing_Low-Pulley_One-Arm_Triceps_Extension, Kneeling_Cable_Triceps_Extension) are all upright pushdowns or overhead extensions, none bent over.
curator.why: The implement is wrong: a dumbbell kickback is not a cable kickback. With dumbbells, gravity loads the arm in a different direction and there is no cable line. None of the cable triceps exercises use a bent-over posture with the upper arm parallel to the floor and the elbow extending backward. Searches for 'kickback' and for bent-over cable instructions found only a glute kickback (One-Legged_Cable_Kickback) and shoulder exercises.

curator.photoShows: Cable_Wrist_Curl: seated on a bench, forearms on the thighs, a low-pulley straight bar held palms up. Frame 0 has the wrists hanging over the knees and frame 1 has them curled up, so this is wrist flexion. Seated_Two-Arm_Palms-Up_Low-Pulley_Wrist_Curl: the same set-up with a palms-up bar curled toward the body, also wrist flexion.
curator.why: Both cable wrist exercises use a supinated (palms-up) grip and train the wrist flexors. A wrist extension needs a palms-down grip and lifts the back of the hand. Copying these frames would train the opposite muscle group. The palms-down wrist curls in the source all use a dumbbell or barbell, which is the wrong implement for a cable exercise.

curator.photoShows: Weighted_Squat: standing on two flat benches with a dip belt and a plate hanging on a chain between the legs, arms forward; standing, then a squat. Cable_Deadlifts: standing between low pulleys holding two handles at the sides; squatted down, then standing.
curator.why: There is no cable belt squat in the source. Weighted_Squat is a belt squat, but the load is a plate hanging from a dip belt, not a low-pulley cable attached to a belt, so the implement is wrong. Cable_Deadlifts uses cables, but the load is held in the hands on two handles at the sides, with no belt.

curator.photoShows: Goblet_Squat: kettlebell held at the chest, standing, then a deep squat. Cable_Deadlifts: two low-pulley handles held at the sides, squatted, then standing.
curator.why: The source has no cable squat with a single handle held at the chest. Goblet_Squat uses a kettlebell (wrong implement). Cable_Deadlifts uses cables, but the handles hang at the sides (wrong hold and loading position). A keyword search for 'squat' among cable exercises returns 0 hits.

curator.photoShows: Cable_Deadlifts: two low-pulley handles held at the sides, squatted, then standing. Weighted_Squat: plate on a dip belt.
curator.why: The source has no cable squat with the handles or bar held in a front-rack position. Its only cable squatting movement (Cable_Deadlifts) holds the handles at the sides. Front squats in the source (Front_Barbell_Squat, Front_Squat_Clean_Grip, Front_Squats_With_Two_Kettlebells) use barbells or kettlebells, not cables.

curator.photoShows: Pull_Through: facing away from a low pulley with the rope between the legs. Frame 0: hinged with arms straight, reaching back between the thighs. Frame 1: standing tall with the rope at the groin. Band_Good_Morning: a band looped behind the neck and stood on, hinged then upright. Cable_Deadlifts: two low handles held at the sides, squat-down then stand.
curator.why: A good morning loads the upper back or chest while the athlete hinges. Pull_Through has the load in straight arms passing between the legs, which is a different exercise and has its own name. Band_Good_Morning has the right pattern but uses a band, not a cable. Cable_Deadlifts is a squat-style deadlift with handles at the sides. No source photo shows a cable good morning.

curator.photoShows: Kettlebell_One-Legged_Deadlift: one-leg hinge with a kettlebell in one hand. Frame 0: standing. Frame 1: hinged with the free leg extended back. Cable_Deadlifts: two-leg squat-style deadlift with two low cable handles. Pull_Through: two-leg cable hinge with a rope between the legs.
curator.why: The single-leg hinge photo uses a kettlebell, which is the wrong implement for a cable exercise. Both cable hinge photos are two-leg, which is the wrong laterality. The source has no cable single-leg deadlift.

The source has no cable march or cable-resisted gait. The closest, the harness sled drag, uses a different implement (sled) and is a sprint, not a march. curator.photoShows: Hip_Flexion_with_Band: standing, facing away from a low anchor, with an elastic band (not a cable) cuffed to one ankle. curator.photoShows: Dead_Bug: a woman lying on her back on the floor, bodyweight only, arms straight up toward the ceiling, hips and knees at 90 degrees in frame 0; frame 1 extends one leg toward the floor. No cable or handle.

curator.photoShows: Cable from the LOW pulley of a dual cable tower, one standard handle held with both hands, standing side-on to the tower. Frame 0: arms extended down and across toward the low pulley at hip height. Frame 1: handle pulled up and diagonally across the body to straight arms above the far shoulder, torso rotated, back foot pivoted. This is a low-to-high diagonal chop.
curator.why: A reverse chop is the low-to-high cable wood chop (also called a cable lift). Standing_Cable_Lift has the same implement (cable, single handle held with both hands), both arms, a standing position and a rotational low-to-high diagonal path, exactly as its instructions describe. Standing_Cable_Wood_Chop is the high-to-low chop, the opposite direction, so it was rejected. Cable_Judo_Flip (rope, pulled over the shoulder and downward) and Pallof_Press_With_Rotation (horizontal press) are different patterns.

reviewers.reason: I viewed both frames. Implement: a cable from a Freemotion dual cable cross. The cable runs from the pulley at the bottom of the swing arm, about knee or shin height, so it is a low pulley. Handle: one D-handle held with both hands. Laterality: two hands on one handle, which fits a chop. Body position: standing with feet about shoulder width, no kneeling, no split stance and no support surface. The athlete stands at an angle to the tower. In frame 0 the arms are extended down in front of the hips toward the low pulley. In frame 1 the handle has been pulled up and diagonally across the body to straight arms above the shoulder away from the tower. The torso is rotated away and the rear foot is pivoted on its toes. That is a low-to-high diagonal rotation. The app defines Cable Reverse Chop with the cue 'upward diagonal trunk-to-arm force transfer' (client/src/lib/exerciseCatalogExpansion.ts:115). It is a separate entry from Cable Wood Chop (#250, high to low) and Cable Horizontal Chop (#378). So the cable lift is the right exercise, and copying these frames gives an upward chop with the correct implement, handle, stance and plane. Minor point: the source text says to squat to the handle, but frame 0 is nearly upright. This does not change the exercise.

I viewed both frames. Frame 0: the athlete stands side-on to a Freemotion dual cable tower, with the cable running from the LOW pulley. He holds one single handle with both hands, arms straight and angled down toward the pulley at hip height, torso square. Frame 1: the handle has been pulled up and diagonally across the body to above the far (left) shoulder with nearly straight arms. The torso is rotated away from the tower and the back foot has pivoted onto its toes. So the photos show a low-to-high diagonal chop: a cable from the low pulley, two hands on one handle, standing, with trunk rotation. That is the standard definition of a reverse (low-to-high) wood chop. The app's own sportCue for #377 is 'upward diagonal trunk-to-arm force transfer', which matches. The photos do not show a high-to-low chop (that is #250, Standing_Cable_Wood_Chop), a horizontal chop, or a straight-arm press or pull. The implement is a cable, the attachment is a single handle, both hands work together on one handle, and the stance is standing, which is the default because the name specifies no kneeling. The movement is a dynamic rep with rotation, not an isometric hold. Someone copying these two frames would perform a cable reverse chop.

curator.photoShows: No source photo shows a standing cable rotation with straight arms moving horizontally at chest height. Standing_Cable_Wood_Chop: standing, high pulley, single handle held in both hands, pulled down and diagonally to the opposite knee. Standing_Cable_Lift: low pulley, pulled diagonally from the hip to above the opposite shoulder. Cable_Russian_Twists: the athlete lies face-up in a bridge on a stability ball with arms vertical, then rotates. Pallof_Press_With_Rotation: both frames show only hands at the chest and then pressed straight out; the rotation is never pictured. Cable_Judo_Flip: low pulley, rope pulled over the shoulder into a bent-over crunch.
curator.why: A horizontal chop is a standing, mid-height cable rotation with the arms sweeping across the body roughly parallel to the floor. Wood Chop was already rejected because its path is diagonal (high to low), and its frames confirm that. Standing Cable Lift is the opposite diagonal (low to high). Cable Russian Twists rotates in the right plane but lying face-up on a ball, not standing. Pallof Press With Rotation includes a horizontal twist in its instructions, but its two frames show only the press-out, so copying them would not teach the chop. Judo Flip is an over-the-shoulder rope pull into a crunch. None of these is the app's exercise.

curator.photoShows: Closest is Shotgun_Row: a standing single-arm low-pulley cable row with a single handle and a wide split stance. Frame 0 shows the arm reaching forward with the shoulder protracted and the torso deeply hinged. Frame 1 shows the elbow pulled back and the wrist supinated while the torso stays hunched forward. Seated_One-arm_Cable_Pulley_Rows is a seated single-handle row with an upright, still torso. Kneeling_Single-Arm_High_Pulley_Row is a kneeling high-pulley pull-down.
curator.why: A cable rotational row is defined by deliberate trunk rotation during the pull: you turn toward the stack on the reach and rotate open as you row, and the obliques are prime movers. Shotgun Row is the nearest single-arm standing cable row, but its source instructions describe only shoulder retraction, elbow flexion and wrist supination, with no trunk rotation. The frames show a heavily hinged low-cable lat row in which any torso turn is incidental. Someone copying it would do a single-arm row, not a rotational row, so it is a near miss on the movement pattern (rotational vs straight). The seated one-arm row and the kneeling high-pulley row have no rotation and use the wrong position. No other cable row in the source shows rotation; Pallof Press With Rotation, Standing Cable Lift and Cable Russian Twists are presses or chops, not rows.

curator.photoShows: Pallof_Press: standing side-on to a mid/low pulley, hands clasped on a chain handle at the chest (frame 0), then arms pressed straight out (frame 1). The feet stay in place and there is no lateral stepping. Pallof_Press_With_Rotation: standing, handle at the chest, then pressed out. Again the feet stay planted.
curator.why: An anti-rotation walkout means holding the cable handle in front of the chest and walking sideways away from the stack and back, resisting rotation while the tension rises. The only anti-rotation cable photos in the source are Pallof presses, a stationary press-out from the chest. That is a different movement (arm press, no walking), so it would be a near miss at best. No source exercise shows a walkout.

curator.photoShows: Single-Arm_Linear_Jammer: one arm presses the landmine bar end from the shoulder to lockout, with the same arm in both frames. Landmine_Linear_Jammer: both hands on a handle attachment, squat-to-press.

The two-handle jammer is simultaneous and bilateral, with a squat. Per the laterality rule, neither shows an alternating press.

curator.photoShows: Both landmine press sources (Single-Arm_Linear_Jammer, Landmine_Linear_Jammer) are performed standing, the second with a squat. No source shows a kneeling landmine press.
curator.why: Body position must be tall-kneeling. Every landmine press photo in the source is standing with leg drive, so it fails on position. A search of all instructions for kneeling presses found only cable or bodyweight exercises (Kneeling Arm Drill, Kneeling Cable Triceps Extension), none of them landmine.

curator.photoShows: Closest is Lying_T-Bar_Row: a plate-loaded chest-supported T-bar row MACHINE. The athlete stands on its angled footplate with his chest on the machine's pad and rows the machine's pivoting lever arm by its handles. Frame 0: arms extended. Frame 1: handles pulled to the chest.
curator.why: The movement (a chest-supported two-arm T-bar row) is close, but the implement differs: the photo shows a dedicated T-bar row machine (source equipment 'machine', with its own frame, footplate and chest pad), not a landmine barbell set up with a bench. The rules list machine vs landmine as different implements, and someone copying the frames would need that machine. The app's own Chest-Supported T-Bar Row (#51) already uses this photo correctly. The other chest-supported rows in the source (Lying Cambered Barbell Row, Incline Bench Pull, Dumbbell Incline Row) are free-barbell or dumbbell rows on a bench, not landmine.

curator.photoShows: The nearest photos are the single-arm landmine rows. Bent_Over_One-Arm_Long_Bar_Row and One-Arm_Long_Bar_Row: the athlete stands beside a one-end-anchored bar with feet parallel and square, and rows it one-handed by gripping the shaft behind the plates, other hand on the knee or thigh.
curator.why: 'Offset' is the defining word of this variation: an asymmetric or offset set-up such as a staggered/offset stance or an offset grip, built for anti-rotation. That is distinct from the plain single-arm landmine row, which is already matched to #256 with these photos. The source photos show a square-stance standard one-arm landmine row with nothing offset visible, and no source exercise names or shows an offset landmine row. Because the variation's defining element cannot be confirmed in any photo, using the base single-arm row would be a near miss.

curator.photoShows: A barbell anchored at one end (landmine), with the athlete holding the free loaded end in both hands, arms extended, in a wide standing stance. Frame 0: trunk and hips rotated to one side, bar end lowered beside that hip. Frame 1: rotated fully to the other side, bar end lowered beside the opposite hip. Two-handed, standing, rotational hip-to-hip arc.
curator.why: The full contact twist (Westside) is a two-handed landmine rotation: hold the bar end at arm's length in front of the face, then rotate the trunk and hips to bring it down to one hip, then the other. The source's Landmine 180s instructions describe exactly this: bar raised to shoulder height with arms extended, wide stance, rotate trunk and hips to swing the weight down to one side, then to the other. Implement (landmine), grip (both hands on the bar end), laterality, standing stance and rotational path all agree. The only reservation is that the photos do not visibly show the rear-foot pivot that some coaches cue for the full contact twist. The hips clearly rotate, and copying the frames produces the right movement. No other landmine rotation exists in the source; Landmine Linear Jammer is a press.

reviewers.reason: I viewed both frames, plus a zoomed crop of the feet. Implement: a loaded Olympic barbell with one end anchored on the floor out of frame to the left, so it is a landmine and not a free barbell. Grip: both hands on the free sleeve end with no handle attachment, which is right for a full contact twist. Laterality: two hands and two legs. Position: standing in a wide, slightly staggered stance with the feet facing the anchor. The feet are planted in exactly the same spot in both frames. Load: a plate is visible on the bar. Movement: in frame 0 the trunk and hips are rotated toward the camera, the arms are nearly straight and the bar end is down by one hip. In frame 1 the trunk and hips have rotated the other way (back to the camera) and the bar end has crossed to the opposite side at about lower-chest height. That is a two-handed, hip-driven rotation from one side to the other. This is the landmine rotation that coaches call the full contact twist, also known as the landmine 180. Someone copying these frames would do the app's exercise. Small differences: frame 1 does not lower the bar all the way to the opposite hip (curator overstated this), and there is no back-foot pivot, which some coaches add. Neither changes the exercise. No other source in the 876-entry list is a closer match; the only other landmine source is the Linear Jammer, which is a press.

I viewed both frames. They show a barbell anchored at one end, out of frame to the lower left, so this is a landmine and not a free barbell. The athlete is standing in a wide, slightly staggered stance and holds the loaded free end of the bar with both hands. In frame 0 his trunk and hips are rotated to his left and the bar end is pulled down beside his left hip. In frame 1 he has turned about 120 to 135 degrees to his right. His back is partly toward the camera, and the bar end is up in front of him at about lower-chest height, slightly to his right. The movement is a two-handed rainbow arc around the anchor, driven by trunk and hip rotation. That is the full contact twist, which coaches widely treat as the same exercise as landmine 180s, landmine rotations or rainbows. It is not a press, a row or a straight-plane chop. Implement, stance, laterality and the rotational pattern all match the app exercise. Two caveats, neither enough to refute. First, the curator's description of frame 1 is wrong: the bar is not lowered beside the opposite hip but held up in front at chest height, so the pair shows one hip side to the front or top of the arc rather than hip to hip. Second, the elbows are fairly bent in both frames and the feet stay planted, whereas the coaching cues for a full contact twist are long arms and a pivot of the back foot. These are technique details within the same exercise, and someone copying the frames would still do a standing two-hand landmine twist.

curator.photoShows: Single-Arm_Linear_Jammer: side view of a standing athlete pressing the landmine bar end with one arm from the shoulder (frame 0) to full extension (frame 1). The feet sit close together with only slight fore-aft offset, the whole body leans into the bar, and the source describes a wide stance with explosive hip and knee drive.
curator.why: This is the closest candidate: a one-arm standing landmine press. But the app name specifies a split stance (one foot well forward, one back, often with the rear knee bent), and the photo shows a wide or near-parallel stance with only a small stagger. It is also a push press with leg drive rather than a strict press. Under the stance rule this is a near miss, so the answer is none.

curator.photoShows: One-Arm_Kettlebell_Clean_and_Jerk: frame 0 has the kettlebell hanging between the legs in a half-squat or hinge; frame 1 has it racked at the shoulder. No overhead frame. Two-Arm_Kettlebell_Military_Press: frame 0 two kettlebells racked; frame 1 both locked out overhead. No clean. One-Arm_Kettlebell_Military_Press_To_The_Side: rack, then single-arm lockout. No clean. One-Arm_Kettlebell_Push_Press: rack, then a dip with the bell still at the shoulder.
curator.why: A clean and press needs both phases visible: a clean from a hang or the floor to the rack, then a strict press overhead. No kettlebell source photographs both. The one-arm clean-and-jerk frames stop at the rack, so they only teach the clean (the app already has 'Kettlebell Clean' on Kettlebell_Dead_Clean), and its finish would be a jerk, not a press. The press-only sources start at the rack with no clean, and the two-arm one is double-bell. Clean_and_Press exists only with a barbell (wrong implement).

curator.photoShows: Barbell_Side_Split_Squat: barbell back-loaded lateral lunge. Goblet_Squat: kettlebell held at the chest by the horns, then a symmetric two-leg deep squat.
curator.why: The source has no lateral squat with a goblet-held kettlebell. Barbell_Side_Split_Squat has the lateral pattern, but the load is a barbell on the back, not a goblet kettlebell. Goblet_Squat has the right implement and hold, but it is a symmetric bilateral squat with no lateral weight shift.

curator.photoShows: No source shows a one-leg take-off from the floor onto a box. Single_Leg_Push-off: one foot already on a low box, then a vertical push-off with a high knee (a box push-off drill). Single-Leg_Stride_Jump: actually shows a leap off a box into a running stride on the floor. Box_Skip: a bounding skip over or between boxes. Front_Box_Jump: a two-foot box jump.
curator.why: A single-leg box jump takes off from one leg on the floor and lands on top of the box. Single_Leg_Push-off starts with the foot on the box and lands back on it, so the athlete never jumps onto the box. That is a different drill. Front_Box_Jump is two-leg (wrong laterality). Box_Skip and Single-Leg_Stride_Jump are alternating-leg bounding drills that leave the box. Single-Leg_Hop_Progression and Single-Leg_Lateral_Hop use cones with no box. None of them shows the exercise.

curator.photoShows: Frame 0: athlete standing tall on a single plyo box, feet together, looking down. Frame 1: athlete has dropped forward off the box and landed on the floor on both feet in an athletic quarter-to-half squat, hips back, arms forward. No target box is visible and no rebound jump is shown. The landing in frame 1 is two-footed.
curator.why: By name, a depth drop to stick means stepping off a box, landing and freezing in an athletic position. The two frames show exactly that: box, then landed position. They do not show the depth jump's rebound. The source is labelled 'Linear Depth Jump', but only its drop-and-land portion is photographed. Confidence is low for two reasons: (1) the app tags this exercise 'unilateral', and a single-leg landing would make this two-foot photo the wrong laterality, although the name does not say single-leg and the standard depth drop is bilateral; (2) frame 1 shows slight arm-motion blur, so the 'stick' is implied rather than clearly frozen. Depth_Jump_Leap shows a similar drop and landing but has a taller target box right in front, which signals a jump, and the app already uses it for 'Depth Jump'. If #394 is meant to be single-leg, the answer is none: no source shows a single-leg drop landing.

reviewers.reason: I viewed both frames. Frame 0 shows the athlete standing tall on a low red plyo box (about 12-16 in) with his feet together, bodyweight only. In frame 1 he has dropped forward and landed on the floor on BOTH feet in a shallow athletic squat, arms forward. The box, set-up and load fit a depth drop, but the laterality does not fit this app exercise. The app defines #394 with quality "unilateral". Its sibling #395 Drop Landing is the one the app labels "bilateral landing and position-control support". So the app separates these two exercises by laterality, and Depth Drop to Stick is the single-leg version. The photo shows only a two-foot landing, so someone copying it would do the bilateral drop landing (#395), not a single-leg stick. That is the 'two-leg photo for a single-leg exercise' case. A second, smaller point: the source is a depth jump, so frame 1 is the turn-around before a rebound, not a held stick. No single-leg drop or landing photo exists in the source list (only Single-Leg Hop Progression, Lateral Hop and similar). If the app's "unilateral" tag is a data error, this photo would fit, but as defined it is not a match.

I viewed both frames. Frame 0 shows the athlete standing on a low red plyo box with his feet together. Frame 1 shows him landed on the floor in front of the box on BOTH feet, heels flat, in a shallow quarter squat with arms forward. That is a two-footed drop landing. The app defines Depth Drop to Stick with the quality 'unilateral', and the neighbouring app exercise #395 Drop Landing is the one cued as 'bilateral landing'. The app therefore separates the two by laterality, and this photo shows only the bilateral one. Someone copying these frames would land on two feet, not stick a single-leg landing. Using the same photo here would also make #394 look identical to #395. The source is also a depth jump (drop then rebound onto a second box), not a drop-to-stick, although the frames themselves stop at the landing. Laterality is wrong, so refute.

reviewers.reason: I viewed both frames. Frame 0: athlete stands on a single low red plyo box with feet together, arms at his sides, unloaded. Frame 1: he has dropped forward off the box (the box is now behind him) and landed on both feet on the floor. His knees and hips are bent in a quarter-to-half squat, his torso leans forward slightly and his arms reach forward for balance. That is the absorbed bilateral landing. Implement (one plyo box), body position (standing on the box, then a floor landing), laterality (two feet) and load (bodyweight) all match the app's Drop Landing, which the app describes as a bilateral landing. No second platform or rebound jump appears in the frames. Copying them gives exactly a drop landing: step off, land on two feet, absorb.

curator.why: A sled march is a heavy sled push on high handles at a deliberate, marching tempo with knee drive. Implement (push sled), grip (high posts), body position (forward lean into the handles) and pattern (alternating-leg resisted gait) all match what the frames show. reviewers.reason: I viewed both frames and enlarged the feet. The implement and grip are right: a loaded push sled with high vertical posts, gripped with both hands, elbows bent, body leaning hard. The gait is wrong. Both frames show sprinting strides. In frame 0 the lead foot is off the turf in swing, the rear leg is fully extended and the push-off is on the toes, the torso is near horizontal and the head is down. The source's instructions say to move 'as fast as you can'. A sled march is a deliberately slow, heavy marching drill: one foot always on the ground, a knee drive followed by a full-foot plant. It is not running. The app already has a separate 'Sled Sprint' (#298) mapped to this same Prowler_Sprint photo, which confirms that the march must look different from the sprint. Someone copying these frames would sprint the sled, so the movement pattern (march vs sprint) does not match. Sled_Push is not a substitute either: it shows a low-handle push with arms extended, not a march.

I viewed both frames and enlarged crops. Both show a loaded push sled on turf with hands on the two high red posts. The torso is very low (about 25-30 degrees above horizontal), the head is tucked down and the elbows are bent. Both frames catch fast, short driving steps: the trailing leg is extended onto the toes and the lead foot is just at or near the ground under the body. This is the source's own exercise, a Prowler SPRINT ('move as fast as you can'), shown in a sprint/drive posture. A coach's Sled March is a different gait: a slow, deliberate resisted march, roughly a 45-degree straight body line with long arms, an exaggerated knee drive with a dorsiflexed ankle, and one foot always grounded. Neither frame shows a high knee drive or a march posture. Someone copying these frames would sprint-push the sled, not march it. Through the movement lens this is a march-vs-sprint cousin, so refute.

curator.photoShows: Battling_Ropes, the only battle-rope source: shirtless athlete in a standing athletic stance holding one rope end in each hand. In frame 0 the right hand is up at shoulder height and the left is low. In frame 1 the hands are reversed. These are alternating waves.
curator.why: A battle rope slam lifts both ropes overhead together and slams them down simultaneously. Battling_Ropes shows alternating single-arm waves, both by its instructions and in both frames, and was already rejected for #399 for exactly this flaw. No other source uses battle ropes. Overhead_Slam and One-Arm_Medicine_Ball_Slam are medicine-ball slams (wrong implement), and Sledgehammer_Swings uses a hammer.
